trials.planText:
A flyer and an outreach plan, pointed at a first Saturday workday in October — that's exactly the right first move. Here's the plan.

# Hartwell Street Garden — Project Plan

## The vision

An empty lot on Hartwell Street becomes the block's shared ground. It starts small and human: a hand-lettered flyer on doors and the corner corkboard, six families becoming ten, and a first Saturday workday in October where people show up with gloves and leave knowing three neighbors they didn't know before. The garden grows food, but the first crop is the relationships — the Community Garden recipe in the commons calls this out directly: gardens build bonding ties among the regulars and bridging ties across age, language, and how long you've lived on the block. That's what we're planting first.

## People & practices

- **Who this serves:** the six interested families first, then the rest of the block — this is a bonding project at its core (deepening ties on one street), with a bridging edge (the flyer invites households nobody has talked to yet).
- **Who tends it:** you, for now — the person who knocks, posts the flyer, and hosts the workday. The Community Garden recipe says a core team of 5–10 makes a garden durable; the outreach plan's real goal is finding your other four or five co-organizers, not just attendees.
- **The practice the artifacts serve:** personal invitation. The flyer is air cover; the door-knock and the group-chat message do the real work. Per the recipe, plan on 6–12 months from first workday to a fully running garden — October is for clearing, meeting, and dreaming together, not planting everything.
- **The workday itself:** someone greets every arrival by name, someone brings coffee, and the day ends with one question asked out loud: "who wants to help plan the next one?"

## Artifacts

**First build**
1. **The flyer** — print-ready, one page: the lot's location, the workday date (first Saturday in October), what to bring, and one line that makes it an invitation, not an announcement ("Help us turn the empty lot into our garden"). A tear-off or text-this-number way to say "count me in."
2. **The outreach plan** — a concrete two-week plan: which doors to knock first (the six families become knockers, not just attendees), where flyers go, what to say in the group chat, and how to follow up with everyone who shows interest before the workday.

**Later**
3. **A landing page** — once there's a workday photo and a growing list, a simple public face for the garden.
4. **The full system** — plot signups, workday scheduling, a harvest board. This earns its turn after the October workday, when there are real people to coordinate — building the login system before the relationships exist is the classic way gardens stall.

Keeping the first build to these two means you're handing out flyers this week, and everything later gets aimed by who actually shows up. All of it lives in this one project.

## Look & feel

The whole thing is a version of **a hand-painted garden sign** — the kind wired to a chain-link fence, lettered with a brush.

- **Ground:** deep green — `#2D5232`
- **Ink:** warm cream — `#F5EFDD` (reversed out of the green, like paint on the sign)
- **Signal color:** marigold — `#E8A33D` — used only for the date and the "count me in" action
- **Type:** *Caprasimo* or *Fredoka* for display (rounded, painted feel) with *Nunito* for body — both on Google Fonts
- **Edge:** soft corners, generous spacing, slightly imperfect — hand-made, not corporate

For the flyer's artwork: a real photo of the Hartwell Street lot beats any stock or AI image — neighbors will recognize their own block. Even better long-term: this garden is a natural first commission for a local artist to paint the actual sign, and the flyer can borrow that lettering. AI art is a placeholder at most.

## The first screen

For the flyer, the three-second test: **GARDEN**, big and painted-feeling, then the date and the lot's address, then one action — text or tear-off. That's it. Deliberately NOT on it: the garden's backstory, a list of rules, a QR code to a form nobody's built yet. A neighbor walking past should get it before they've stopped walking.

## Pages & files

- `flyer.html` — the print-ready flyer (also works on a phone if shared in the group chat)
- `outreach-plan.md` — the two-week plan, written to be printed or shared with the six families

## Data & services

None. Both artifacts are static — no backend, no email service, no env vars. Services enter the picture only when the full system does, later.

PROJECT-NAME: Hartwell Street Garden

From across the sidewalk, three things read instantly: **a garden is starting here**, **the date in red**, **come help**. That's it. Deliberately not on it: a mission paragraph, a list of rules, a QR code maze. If it needs explaining, it's too full.

trials.planText:
Six families and a lot with the owner's blessing — the tech's job here is small: get the flyer on the corkboard and get you knocking on doors before the first Saturday in October. Here's the plan.

## The vision

A hand-painted-looking flyer goes up at the laundromat, the corner store, the school gate, and in six mailboxes on Hartwell Street. It says one thing clearly: **the empty lot is going to be a garden, and we're starting Saturday, October 4th.** A neighbor who has walked past that lot for years — who was never going to fill out a form or join a group chat — reads it in four seconds, remembers the date, and shows up with a rake. By noon there are eleven people on the lot instead of six families, two of them have never spoken before, and the garden exists because people were standing on it together.

The flyer does the inviting. The outreach plan makes sure the flyer isn't doing it alone.

## People & practices

**Who this serves.** Two kinds of connection at once, and the garden is unusually good at both — the Community Garden recipe in the commons names this directly: gardens build **bonding** capital among the regulars, **bridging** capital across age, race, class, and language, and **linking** capital to schools, pantries, and the city. Your six families are the bonding core. The flyer's real work is bridging: reaching the households nobody has asked yet.

**Who tends it.** You, by name, on the flyer. A first workday with no visible host is a first workday people drive past. One phone number or email, yours, and a line that says who to ask.

**The practices this depends on:**
- **Personal invitation beats paper.** The commons recipe puts a new garden's core organizing team at 5–10 people — you have that. Your six families should each invite one household directly, in person or by text. The flyer catches the people none of you know; the ask catches the people you do.
- **The workday is the tool.** Everything points at one date and one place. No signup required to attend — showing up is the signup.
- **Collect names on the day, not before.** A clipboard at the lot on October 4th (name, phone, "what I'd like to grow") is worth more than any form, and it's what tells you whether you need software at all.
- **Two practical things to settle before you print.** Get the owner's permission in writing, even a short signed note — a season of work on someone's lot deserves that. And find out where the water comes from. Both belong in your outreach plan as tasks, not on the flyer.

One note on timing: the recipe puts a new garden at 6–12 months to launch. October 4th isn't planting day — it's the clearing, measuring, and sheet-mulching day, and the day the group becomes a group. Naming it as "first workday" rather than "garden opening" keeps expectations honest and the momentum real.

## Artifacts

### First build
1. **The flyer** — print-ready, 8.5×11, designed to read from four feet away on a corkboard: garden name, the lot's address on Hartwell Street, Saturday October 4th with a time, "bring gloves if you have them," your name and number. Black-and-white-photocopy-safe as well as color.
2. **The outreach plan** — a short, concrete two-week plan: the six families' invitation assignments, the eight or ten places to post the flyer in walking distance, a text message you can paste and send, a door-knock script for the houses you don't know, and the pre-workday checklist (written permission, water, tools, a clipboard).

### Later
- **A landing page** — one page with the date, the story, and a "count me in" that collects an email. Earns its turn once more people are asking about the garden than you can text back.
- **The full system** — plot or bed assignments, workday rosters, harvest sharing, a garden calendar. This is real and worth building, but only after a few workdays have happened and you know how your group actually decides things. The commons **Block Party Organizing** prompt is the right shape to borrow when you get there: role cards with spots-filled counts, and a steward roster you can export. Building it now would mean designing rules for a group that hasn't met yet.

## Look & feel

**The real-world object:** a hand-painted sign nailed to the fence at the edge of the lot. Not a poster, not a startup announcement — a sign someone made with a brush. That means the layout is a few big elements stacked with air between them, slightly off-perfect, and no columns or boxes.

- **Ground:** deep garden green, `#22402F`
- **Ink:** warm chalky cream, `#F3EAD3` — the painted lettering
- **Signal color:** tomato red, `#C4472A` — used for exactly one thing, the date
- **Type pairing:** **Fraunces** for the display lines (a soft, warm serif with a hand-cut feel — set it large and heavy) with **Karla** for the details. Both on Google Fonts.
- **Edge:** soft. Rounded corners, no hairline rules, generous margins, nothing boxed in. Dense enough to read fast, airy enough to feel unhurried.

**On artwork:** the strongest version of this flyer has a photo of the actual lot on it — the weeds, the fence, the light. Take one on your phone this week. And if someone on Hartwell Street paints, letters, or draws, ask them to make the garden's sign and its logo — paid, if you can manage it. The garden becomes a reason to hire your neighborhood's artists, and the flyer will look like nowhere else. Anything I generate is a placeholder standing in until that happens.

## The first screen

Seen from four feet away on a corkboard: the garden's name in big painted letters, **SATURDAY OCTOBER 4** in tomato red beneath it, and the Hartwell Street address. That's the whole top half. A reader who glances and walks on still leaves with the date and the place — which is the flyer's entire job.

Deliberately not on it: a paragraph explaining what a community garden is, a QR code as the primary action, a list of rules or plot fees, a website URL that doesn't exist yet, or any logo but the garden's. If the flyer needs explaining, the flyer is wrong.

## Pages & files

- A single flyer page, laid out at print size with proper print margins and a clean print stylesheet
- A second page holding the outreach plan — readable on your phone, printable as a one-pager to hand to the other five families
- One shared stylesheet carrying the palette, fonts, and edge treatment, so the landing page and eventual system inherit the same look

## Data & services

Nothing. No backend, no email service, no accounts — these are two printable pages. Your database for the next month is a clipboard. When the landing page arrives and starts collecting "count me in" emails, that's when we add Community Cloud storage and Resend, and I'll name the env vars then.

---

Good — that gives me enough. A flyer and an outreach plan pointed at one real date, in the language of a painted garden sign.

# Hartwell Street Garden — Project Plan

## The vision

It's the first Saturday in October, mid-morning. The empty lot on Hartwell Street has eight people standing in it who don't all know each other yet — the six families who said they were interested, plus three households who saw a green flyer taped inside the laundromat window and figured they'd walk over. Someone brought a wheelbarrow, someone brought a thermos, someone's kid is already pulling up weeds with a bare hand. Nobody logged in to anything. The flyer said *Saturday, October 4, 10am, the empty lot on Hartwell — the owner said yes, come see what we could do here*, and that was enough.

That's what we're building toward right now: not a garden management system, but the two paper-and-words artifacts that turn "about six families seem interested" into a specific number of specific people standing on a specific piece of dirt on a specific morning.

## People & practices

**This is a bonding project with a bridging edge.** The six interested families are the bonding core — they already know each other enough to say yes. The bridging work is the households on your block you *haven't* talked to: the renters, the elders who don't come to things, the family whose first language isn't yours, the person who's lived there twenty years and has strong opinions about that lot. A flyer is a bridging instrument. It reaches people a group chat never will.

The **Community Garden** recipe in the commons is blunt about the timeline: 6 to 12 months to launch a new garden, with a core organizing team of 5 to 10 people. You have the team and you have the land — which is the hard part. What it also says is worth designing around: gardens generate *linking* capital too, connections to schools, food pantries, and public health folks. Don't chase that yet, but know it's coming.

Three practices this needs, none of which are software:

- **Two hosts, not one.** Before the flyer goes out, ask one of the six families to co-host the October workday with you. It halves the chance this becomes "that one neighbor's garden project" — the most common way these stall.
- **The six families become inviters, not attendees.** When you talk to each of them, the ask isn't "will you come," it's "will you bring one household who isn't on this list." That's what makes the workday bigger than the group chat.
- **Get the owner's yes in writing.** One short note or email from the lot owner saying you may use the land through the season. You'll never need to show it to anyone, but "the owner said yes" printed on a flyer is the sentence that converts skeptics — and you should be able to back it.

## Artifacts

**First build**

1. **The flyer** — print-ready, deep green, readable from four feet away. One version at 8.5×11 for corkboards and windows, one half-page version for door-to-door handing and taping. Content: the garden name, the date and time, "the empty lot on Hartwell St," the line that the owner has given permission, one sentence about what the morning is (looking at the lot together, clearing what's clearable, deciding what's next), and one contact — a phone number to text, not just a QR code.

Here's the plan, shaped around the October workday and the hand-painted sign look.

## The vision

It's late September on Hartwell Street. A cream-colored flyer with painted green lettering shows up on the corkboard at the corner store, taped inside the laundromat window, and in six mailboxes — plus a few more doors than six, because the point of a flyer is the households you *haven't* talked to yet. It says one thing clearly: **the empty lot at [address] is becoming a garden, and we're clearing it together the first Saturday in October, 10am.** No app to download, no form to fill out. By that Saturday, eleven people are standing in the lot with rakes, and two of them have lived four doors apart for six years without knowing each other's names. The garden isn't built. But the group that will build it now exists, and it has met once.

## People & practices

**Who it's for.** Two circles at once, and the flyer has to serve both. The six interested families are the **bonding** circle — already warm, already saying yes, and what they need is a date and a task. Everyone else on the block is the **bridging** circle — the renter, the older neighbor who gardens alone in a back yard, the family who moved in last spring. They need a low-stakes first move: show up for two hours, bring nothing, leave whenever.

**Who tends it.** You, for now. The Community Garden recipe in the commons is clear that a new garden wants a **core organizing team of 5 to 10** — not one hero — and that gardens typically take **6 to 12 months from first meeting to first harvest**. So the real goal of the October workday isn't a cleared lot. It's finding the three or four people who'll become that core team with you. Plan to notice who stays late and ask them directly.

**Practices the artifacts depend on:**
- **Personal invitation beats paper.** Flyers reach the people you can't knock on. For the six interested families, send the message yourself, by name. The outreach plan below separates these two tracks on purpose.
- **A named host at the gate.** On the day, someone (you) stands at the lot entrance and greets every arrival by name-and-introduction. This is the single practice that turns a workday into bridging rather than six families gardening near each other.
- **One thing to bring, and it's not tools.** Ask people to bring a jug of water or something to snack on. Small contributions are how strangers stop feeling like guests.
- **Say what happens next before people leave.** Announce the second date at the first gathering, out loud, while everyone's standing there.

The commons recipe also notes gardens build **linking** capital — to schools, food pantries, public health, the city. Not yet. Note it for month three, when you have a group and a name and something to point at.

## Artifacts

**First build**
1. **The block flyer** — one page, print-ready, black-and-white-photocopy-safe as well as color. Carries: what's happening (a garden, on this lot), the owner's blessing (this matters enormously for legitimacy — "the owner has said yes" stops the "is this allowed?" question cold), the date and time, what to bring, and one way to reach you. Designed for a corkboard, a window, and a mailbox.
2. **The outreach plan** — a concrete two-week sequence: the personal messages to the six families (with draft text in your voice), where the ~25 flyers go and in what order, the two doors worth knocking instead of papering, a reminder message two days before, and what to say at the lot on the day. Includes the "ask three people to stay late" move for building the core team.

Keeping the first build to these two is the point, not a limitation: they're the only things that change what happens on the first Saturday in October, and you can have them in hand this week.

**Later**
- **A landing page** — worth making once the flyer needs somewhere to point beyond your phone number, probably right after the first workday when you have photos of actual neighbors in the actual lot. Far more persuasive than anything designed before the fact.
- **The full system** — plot signups, watering rotation, workday volunteer roles (the Block Party Organizing prompt in the commons has a good pattern for shift cards with spots-available counts, worth borrowing when the time comes), a shared calendar. This earns its turn when coordination actually hurts — when the watering schedule is failing in a group chat, usually a couple of months into the first growing season. Building it now would be building infrastructure for a group that doesn't exist yet.

Everything lives in this one project, so the flyer, the page, and the eventual system stay one thing that grows.

## Look & feel

A hand-painted garden sign — but printed on paper, so it reads as *made by a neighbor*, not designed by an agency.

- **Real-world object:** a hand-lettered wooden sign at the edge of a lot. This drives the layout as much as the palette: stacked centered lines, big at the top, a hand-drawn rule under the headline, generous margins like unpainted wood showing at the edges. Not a poster grid, not columns.
- **Ground:** `#F4EDDC` — warm cream, like unbleached paper stock. Prints cheaply and honestly.
- **Ink:** `#1E3A2B` — deep garden green, near-black at a glance, unmistakably green up close.
- **Signal color:** `#C4552F` — a tomato red-orange, used for exactly one thing: **the date and time.** Nothing else gets it.
- **Type:** **Fraunces** for the display lines (it has a slightly wobbly, cut-by-hand quality that reads as painted rather than typeset), **Karla** for body text and details. Both on Google Fonts.
- **Edge:** soft. Hand-drawn rules rather than straight hairlines, rounded corners on any boxes, airy rather than dense — one line of text should never look crowded by the next.

**On artwork:** the best flyer illustration here is either a photo you take of the actual lot as it is now (weeds and all — "this becomes a garden" is a great before-picture) or a small drawing commissioned from someone on or near your block. If there's a teenager on Hartwell who draws, or a neighbor who paints, this is a reason to knock on their door — the flyer becomes a first collaboration instead of a broadcast. I can put a placeholder mark in the meantime.

## The first glance (the flyer's three seconds)

A neighbor standing at the corkboard, not looking for a project, reads three things before deciding to keep reading: **A GARDEN ON HARTWELL STREET** at the top, the tomato-red date underneath it, and *Saturday, 10am — come for an hour, bring nothing* below that. That's the whole job.

Deliberately not on it: a paragraph about why community gardens matter, a mission statement, a list of six families' names, a QR code to a form, a logo. Anything that needs explaining is a thing to cut, not a thing to word better — the lot, the date, and the open door are enough.

## Pages & files

- `flyer.html` — the print-ready flyer, sized for US Letter, designed to hold up in black-and-white
- `outreach-plan.md` — the two-week sequence with draft message text you can copy into your phone

## Data & services

None. No backend, no email service, no accounts. These are a printable page and a document — nothing to log into, nothing to store. When the landing page arrives and starts collecting "count me in" signups, that's the point where we'd add a backend (Community Cloud) and email (Resend), and not before.

# Block Lending Board

## The vision

A neighbor needs a ladder for one Saturday. Instead of scrolling back through 400 group chat messages or driving to the hardware store, they open the board and see a tan corkboard of pinned cards: *Offering — 8ft ladder*, *Offering — two folding tables*, *Asking — anyone have a stud finder?* They tap a card, see whose it is, and knock on a door two houses down. The group chat stays the group chat; the board is where the stuff lives so it stops getting lost. This is the drill math the **Tool Library** recipe names: a block of 40 households owns 40 drills that each run 12 minutes a year — one shared drill and a porch handoff does the job and makes an introduction.

## People & practices

- **Who it's for:** everyone on the block, starting with the people already in the group chat — that chat is the distribution channel, and a single link posted there is the launch.
- **Who tends it:** you, lightly — welcoming new posts, nudging stale ones, being the person who answers "how does this work?" The board needs a tender more than a moderator, since any neighbor can post directly.
- **The practice around it:** the handoff is the point. The board makes the match; the porch makes the neighbor. Worth seeding the board yourself with 3–4 real offers before sharing the link, so the first visitor sees a board with things on it, not an empty corkboard.
- **Where this can go:** the Tool Library recipe shows the mature form — hundreds of these now exist across North America, some with workshops and classes. If the board takes off, that's the path; the board is the two-family start. The **Community Supplies** prompt in the commons maps a fuller version (photos, categories, condition tags) worth borrowing from later.

## Features

**First build** — the one loop the board exists for:
- The board: all cards visible on load, offers and asks mixed, newest first
- Pin a card: offer or ask, item name, a line of detail, your name and rough location ("blue house near the corner")
- Mark a card *borrowed* or *taken down* so the board stays true

**Later:** photos on cards, categories and search (the board has to earn filters by getting full first), a borrow log ("who has the ladder right now"), gentle reminders for long loans, and the tool-library evolution if the block wants it. Keeping the first build this small isn't a downgrade — it arrives in minutes, you and a few neighbors react to the real thing, and the second build is aimed by what actually happens on the board.

## Look & feel

The board is a version of **the corkboard at the hardware store** — that decides the layout: a field of pinned cards, not a feed or a list.

- **Ground:** plywood tan, `#C9A876`, with cards in off-white paper `#F7F3E8`
- **Ink:** near-black walnut, `#2B2118`
- **Signal color:** hardware-store red, `#B5432E` — used only to mark *Asking* cards so asks pop off the board
- **Type:** **Allerta Stencil** for headings and card titles (the sturdy stencil), **Libre Franklin** for body
- **Edge:** square-cornered cards with a soft drop shadow like paper pinned an inch off the board; a small pin dot at the top of each card; airy spacing so the board reads at a glance

All of this comes straight from your corkboard answer. If you have a photo of an actual corkboard or storefront on your block you love, attach it — real reference beats my hexes. And if the board ever wants a header illustration or a printable flyer to recruit posters, the move is a photo of the block itself or a commission from a local artist, not stock art.

## The first screen

The board, immediately: pinned cards fill the screen, and one button — **Pin something** — sits at the top. Deliberately not on it: no welcome banner, no how-it-works page, no sign-up wall before you can look, no search bar or category filters until the board is full enough to need them.

## Pages & files

- `index.html` — the board and the pin-a-card form (one page is the whole tool)
- `styles.css` — the corkboard brief above
- `app.js` — loading, pinning, and marking cards

Needs a small backend so cards persist and every neighbor sees the same board: **Community Cloud (Supabase)** with one `cards` table (type, item, detail, name, location, status, created_at). Env vars: `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`. No email, no scraping, no logins in the first build — a name typed on the card is enough trust for one block.

trials.planText:
Heard: any neighbor can pin something up, and it looks like the corkboard at the hardware store. Here's the plan.

# Block Lending Board

## The vision
Someone types "does anyone have a ladder?" into the block group chat — and instead of the question scrolling away by dinnertime, someone replies with a link. On the board are eleven things: Dave's 8-foot ladder, two folding tables from the couple on the corner, a wheelbarrow, a carpet cleaner, a canopy tent, a post-hole digger nobody remembers buying. Each card says what it is, whose it is, and how to reach them. The borrowing itself happens the way it always has — a text, a walk down the sidewalk, a ladder handed over a fence — and the board's whole job is to remember what the block owns so the group chat doesn't have to.

The [Tool Library](#) recipe in the commons puts the math plainly: a household uses its drill about 12 minutes a year, so 200 households own 200 idle drills. That recipe also names the cost of doing it properly — 6 to 12 months, a founding team of 3 to 6, a secure space with shelving, 5 to 15 hours a week of stewarding. This is the version that skips all of that: the tools stay in their own garages, and only the *knowledge* of them becomes shared.

## People & practices
**Who it's for:** the households already in your block group chat, first. It grows by the group chat and by word of mouth, not by discovery.

**Who tends it:** you, lightly. Three practices do most of the work here, and none of them are software:

- **Seed it before you share it.** An empty board reads as a dead board. Pin up 6–10 of your own things first — including one slightly embarrassing item, because that gives permission — then post the link.
- **Answer chat questions with the link.** Every time someone asks for something in the group chat, that's the moment: reply, and add the item if it turns up. This is the habit that makes the board real; without it the board is a website, with it the board is where the block keeps its stuff.
- **Say the norms out loud once, in your own voice, in the chat.** Return it clean, return it when you said you would, tell the owner if you break it. These belong in your message to neighbors, not in a terms-of-service page on the site.

One caution from the commons: the **Community Supplies** prompt describes a full sharing platform with a hero section, a three-step "How It Works," category and condition and zip-code filters, and sign-up with referral. That's a good design for a platform serving many neighborhoods. For one block with a group chat, every one of those pieces is a door between a neighbor and a ladder. We're leaving them out on purpose.

## Features

**First build** — the one loop: see what's on the block, pin something up, reach the owner.

- **The board.** All items on one screen as pinned cards: item name, a photo if there is one, whose it is, and their contact. Newest pinned at top.
- **Pin something up.** A short form — what it is, your name, how to reach you, optional photo, optional note ("2-day loan is fine, text before 9pm"). No account.
- **Asks.** The same form with a toggle: an ask is a card too, marked in red, that comes down when it's answered. So "looking for a tile saw for Saturday" has somewhere to live besides the chat.
- **Take it down.** Anyone can remove their own card with the link they get after posting — no admin queue, no approval.

Keeping the first build this small is not a downgrade: it's a draft you can put in the group chat this week and react to. Almost everything below gets better after you've watched ten real neighbors use it, and the second build is where the ambition lands — aimed by what actually happened instead of what we guessed.

**Later**
- Borrowed/available status on a card, if people actually want it (many blocks don't — the text message already says it)
- A lightweight block passphrase or magic-link sign-in, once there's more on the board than you'd want a stranger reading
- Categories or search, once there are enough items that scanning fails — not before
- A printed card for the real corkboard, and a short flyer for the households not in the group chat
- A "who's borrowed what" history, if the block ever wants to see how much use it's getting

## Look & feel
**The real-world object:** the corkboard inside the door at a hardware store — index cards and business cards pinned at slight angles, layered, a little crowded, unmistakably made by hand. This decides the layout, not just the colors: cards of *uneven* height in a dense masonry grid, each with a visible pushpin, a faint drop shadow, and a 1–2° rotation. Not a tidy grid of equal rectangles.

- **Ground:** plywood tan, `#D9C39C`, with a subtle paper/board grain. Cards sit on it in off-white `#F7F2E7`.
- **Ink:** near-black brown-black, `#241F19`. Secondary details in `#6B6055`.
- **Signal color:** hardware-store red, `#C0402B` — used for exactly one thing: asks. Offers are ink on cream; asks are stamped red. Nothing else gets to be red.
- **Type:** **Staatliches** for the board header and item names — condensed, stencil-adjacent, the lettering on a lumber-aisle sign. **Work Sans** for everything else, at a comfortable reading size.
- **Edge:** square corners, hairline rules, dense spacing. No rounded cards, no gradients, no soft shadows besides the small hard one under each pinned card.

**Artwork:** the header should be a hand-lettered "LENDING BOARD" rather than a font, and item photos should be your neighbors' actual phone photos of the actual ladder in the actual garage — that's what makes this look like your block and not a template. For the hand-lettering, the recommended path is a local sign painter, letterer, or art student on your block — the tool becomes a reason to hire a neighbor. A generated or typeset header is a placeholder on the way there.

## The first screen
The board itself, loaded — cards visible above the fold, red asks mixed in with cream offers, with the hand-lettered header sitting small at the top and a single pushpin-styled button: **Pin something up**. A neighbor who opens the link cold understands in three seconds because they've seen this object their whole life.

Deliberately not on it: no hero section, no welcome paragraph, no "How It Works" steps, no sign-in, no category filters, no zip code field, no empty-state illustration. If a neighbor needs a paragraph to understand a corkboard, the corkboard has failed.

## Pages & files
- `app/page.tsx` — the board
- `app/pin/page.tsx` — the post form (offer or ask)
- `app/item/[id]/page.tsx` — single card view, with the owner's take-it-down link
- `components/ItemCard.tsx`, `components/PinButton.tsx`, `components/BoardHeader.tsx`
- `app/api/items/route.ts` — create, list, delete
- `lib/db.ts`, `app/globals.css` (the palette and type live here)

## Data & services
- **Backend: yes.** Community Cloud (Supabase) for one `items` table — id, kind (offer/ask), title, note, owner name, contact, photo URL, edit token, created_at — plus Supabase Storage for photos. Env vars: `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`.
- **Email: no.** Neighbors reach each other by the contact on the card, and the block chat carries notifications. Nothing to send.
- **Scraping: no.**
- **Auth: none in the first build** — this is my proposal, and easy to change. The link lives in your group chat, and posting requires only a name and a contact; each poster gets a private edit link for their own card. The moment the board holds things you wouldn't want a passer-by reading, we add a block passphrase.

The commons is full of people who started exactly where you are, and the pattern that comes up again and again: the smallest possible practice, done in public, repeatedly, beats any app.

Three genuinely different directions this could go:

**Sit outside on purpose.** The *Porch Conversations* recipe is the lowest-energy practice in the whole commons — a chair out front, 20 minutes at a time, until people passing start to slow down. It takes weeks, requires nothing, and produces more neighbor relationships than almost anything else. No build needed; maybe never.

**Become the block's quiet connector.** The *Block Stewards* recipe: one committed neighbor who learns names, notices who has a ladder and who has a new baby, and makes introductions. The tech serves the practice, not the other way around.

**Make the street itself the invitation.** *Intersection Repair*, pioneered by Portland's City Repair Project — neighbors paint a mural in the intersection, add a bench or a tiny library, and the act of building it together does as much as the result. Bigger lift, but it turns "nobody knows each other" into "we made this."
